claim: The capstone project's prevalence in engineering programs rose from about 3% of academic institutions in the 1970s to roughly 66-75% of engineering programs today.
stance_target: historical adoption rate of the capstone/major project model in engineering education
scope_conditions: engineering programs broadly, citing Hauhart & Grahe 2015
quoted_support: In the 1970s, the capstone project was included in only 3% of all academic institutions. In the 1980s and 1990s there was a sharp rise in its popularity, and in the past few years, researchers estimate that the project is suggested or required in about 66%-75% of all engineering programs.

claim: The capstone project's structure has remained largely unchanged over the decades despite Industry 4.0 transformations, with most changes limited to project topics rather than process or structure.
stance_target: capstone/major project pedagogy has not kept pace with industrial and technological change
quoted_support: it appears that the project has hardly changed at academic institutions over the years, aside from slight adaptations, and most of the changes are in the project topics rather than in its essence or structure.

claim: The typical capstone project process moves through theme selection, market/literature review, development of design alternatives, prototype building, testing and analysis, conclusions, and final product/presentation.
stance_target: canonical milestone structure of an engineering capstone/major project
scope_conditions: engineering capstone project process, generalized across institutions
quoted_support: Theme Selection, Market/Literature Research (review), Development of Alternatives, Models/prototype, Tests and Analyzes, Conclusions, Final Product/Presentation

claim: Approximately 75% of engineering students work during their studies, and about 50% of those work in the professional field of their studies, as one mechanism narrowing the academia-industry skills gap.
stance_target: how internships/work experience supplement capstone projects in closing the academia-industry gap
quoted_support: Approximately 75% of engineering students work during their studies, 50% of those work in the professional field of their studies

claim: Key incongruences between academia's capstone model and industry include underweighting non-functional product requirements (innovation, UX, emotional/subjective features), lack of user-centered design emphasis, and absence of modern development methods like Agile and Lean.
stance_target: specific mechanisms of the academia-industry gap in engineering project-based courses
scope_conditions: product development-focused capstone projects (mechanical engineering case, generalizable)
quoted_support: Product requirements: not only functionality and reliability, but also innovation, user experience, and subjective and emotional features... Innovative thinking methods and new development processes: such as the AGILE and LEAN methods.

claim: Some researchers have called for outright cancellation of the capstone project given questions about its continuing relevance since the early 2000s.
stance_target: the capstone/major project remains a justified centerpiece of engineering curricula
quoted_support: In recent years its future has been discussed, and some researchers are calling for cancellation of the entire project (Saar, 2011).
